lessons.title: Coordinating promotional activities
lessons.html:
The coordinator's role

A promotional coordinator plans and synchronises promotional activities across a store, department or group of branches, so that they support the marketing plan rather than competing with each other. In an agri business this might include a calendar of seasonal specials, supplier-funded promotions, farmers' days, agricultural show stands, radio campaigns and in-store demonstrations.

Building the promotional calendar

Start from the farming year and the marketing plan. For each period, decide the theme, the products, the mechanism and the channels.

PeriodThemeExample activities
Late winterPlanting preparationEarly-order fertiliser and seed deals, planter maintenance day
Early summerCrop protection and animal healthTick and fly control campaign, sprayer calibration clinic
AutumnHarvest and storageGrain bags, storage hygiene, scale servicing
WinterLivestock nutritionLick and feed promotion, nutrition talk by feed company

Coordinating stakeholders

  • Suppliers: agree funding, stock, materials, presenters and claim procedures in writing.
  • Buyers: confirm stock levels and delivery timing.
  • Branch managers and staff: communicate plans early; allocate responsibilities.
  • Finance: budgets, pricing loads, supplier claims.
  • External partners: show organisers, radio stations, printers, venues.

Avoiding conflicts

Check that promotions do not overlap in ways that confuse customers or cannibalise margin, for example two competing lick brands discounted in the same week, or a branch-level special undercutting a group campaign.

lessons.title: Managing resources and execution
lessons.html:
Resources

  • Budget: track committed and actual spend per activity. Include advertising, printing, display materials, venue, catering, staff overtime, prizes and transport.
  • People: schedule staff for events and peak sales periods; brief and train them.
  • Materials: posters, shelf talkers, banners, flyers, branded gazebos; manage stock of materials and their return after events.
  • Stock: ensure promoted lines are allocated to branches according to expected demand.

Communication pack

For each promotion, send branches a pack in good time: objective, dates, products and codes, prices, mechanism and rules, display guide, staff talking points and FAQs, and contact person.

Event coordination

For a farmers' day or show stand:

  1. Book the venue or stand and confirm requirements: power, water, shade, parking for bakkies and trailers.
  2. Arrange presenters and topics that farmers value.
  3. Plan logistics: transport of equipment and stock, set-up and strike times.
  4. Plan safety: an emergency plan, first aid kit and first aider, fire extinguishers, barriers around equipment demonstrations, and no handling of hazardous chemicals by the public.
  5. Arrange registration to capture attendance, with consent for future contact under POPIA.

Monitoring execution

Check that branches implement promotions correctly: signage up on time, correct prices at the till, displays built to guide. Use photographs, store visits and reports. Correct problems quickly and share good practice between branches.

Legal compliance

Promotional competitions, advertising claims and pricing must comply with the Consumer Protection Act 68 of 2008. Product claims for agricultural remedies must stay within the registered label.

lessons.title: Evaluating the promotional programme
lessons.html:
Measuring each activity

For each activity, compare results with its objective: sales uplift against a baseline, GP achieved, cost, return on investment, number of attendees, leads generated and new accounts opened.

Return on investment (ROI) = (incremental gross profit − promotion cost) / promotion cost × 100. Example: incremental GP R60,000 and cost R20,000 gives ROI = 40,000 / 20,000 × 100 = 200%.

Evaluating the programme as a whole

  • Did the calendar support the marketing plan's objectives?
  • Which mechanisms and channels worked best for which segments?
  • Were there clashes, gaps or periods of overload for staff?
  • Were supplier claims submitted and recovered in full?
  • Was the budget managed within limits?

Feedback

Gather feedback from branch staff, customers and suppliers. Staff often know which promotions confused customers or created extra work for little return.

Reporting and planning ahead

Produce a concise report with results, insights and recommendations, and use it to build next year's calendar. Keep an archive of materials, results and supplier agreements.

Key points

  • Build a promotional calendar from the farming year and the marketing plan.
  • Coordinate suppliers, buyers, branches and finance, with agreements in writing.
  • Send branches a complete communication pack in good time.
  • Plan safety and POPIA consent for events.
  • Evaluate ROI and lessons learned for the next cycle.
